cards.front: What is the purpose of the Gram-Schmidt process applied to a linearly independent set $\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$?
cards.back: It produces an orthogonal set $\{u_1,\dots,u_n\}$ (or orthonormal $\{e_i\}$) that spans exactly the same subspace.

cards.front: State the explicit formula for the first orthogonal vector $u_1$ in Gram-Schmidt.
Give the general formula for the $k$-th orthogonal vector $u_k$ produced by Gram-Schmidt.
How is an orthonormal set obtained once the orthogonal vectors $\{u_i\}$ have been computed?
Outline the complete Gram-Schmidt algorithm steps for vectors $v_1$ to $v_n$.
cards.back: Initialize empty list U. For k=1 to n: compute u_k by subtracting projections onto all previous u_j, append u_k if nonzero.

cards.front: Why is $\langle u_k,u_j\rangle=0$ for all j<k by construction?
cards.back: The subtracted sum equals the orthogonal projection of v_k onto span{u_1,...,u_{k-1}}, leaving a remainder orthogonal to every vector in that span.

cards.front: What occurs during Gram-Schmidt if the input set is linearly dependent?
cards.back: Some u_k equals the zero vector, revealing the dependence and that the set does not form a basis.

cards.front: In which vector spaces does the Gram-Schmidt algorithm work?
cards.back: Any finite-dimensional inner-product space (real or complex), using the given inner product for all projections.
